idiom_name: Ktor application plugin: createApplicationPlugin + onCall/onCallRespond over the call pipeline
implementation_notes: Ktor's plugin API is the framework-side realization: createApplicationPlugin(name) { ... } builds an ApplicationPlugin that is attached declaratively with install(plugin), and the handlers onCall, onCallReceive and onCallRespond fire at the corresponding stages of every call with ApplicationCall as the Context; the lower-level primitive underneath is phase interception on ApplicationCallPipeline (intercept of a named phase such as Plugins), and on(MonitoringEvent(...)) covers application lifecycle events. The classic Interceptor/Dispatcher pair is replaced by the plugin registry plus the pipeline, so the interceptor never chooses where it runs - the phase does. On the JVM the same code base can reuse Jakarta @AroundInvoke interceptors for managed beans; keep Ktor plugins for HTTP-stage interception and let the container handle business-method interception.
pitfalls: A plugin instance is created once per application and shared by all calls, so per-call state must live in call.attributes (as an AttributeKey) and never in plugin fields.

install() order determines handler order, and a handler that responds directly without forwarding to the next stage short-circuits every later phase - intentional for authorization, disastrous by accident.
Handlers run on the pipeline's coroutine context: a blocking JDBC/file call inside onCall stalls the event loop; wrap it in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
Unsubscribing matters for monitoring hooks - a plugin that subscribes on every install without unsubscribing accumulates listeners across test/reload cycles.
